reviewer_note: Reviewed on branch `vercel-deploy-prep`, not `review-gates` as the brief stated; the working tree was clean apart from app/.gitignore. No repo file was modified and the database was not touched. This report is the only file written.

prereg.evidence: `git log --follow` on research-log/critical-paths/chains.json shows bbfa54f as the file's first commit. `git show bbfa54f:research-log/critical-paths/chains.json` contains both paths with "finding": null and "links": []. Chain 1's expectation string is byte-identical to the value now in critical_paths.expectation; chain 2's expectation is likewise identical (only axes_excluded was later reworded). The findings, links, docs/critical-paths.md and the decisions rows all arrive in 1ed9421, four minutes and thirty-seven seconds later. The ordering is real and checkable, exactly as methodology/critical-path.md requires. Two caveats are filed as findings below: git proves the order of the writes, not the order of the thinking, and chain 2's expectation already contains a finding-shaped citation.

findings.target: path-telescope-elapsed-time, links seq 2 and seq 3 — duration labels vs the intervals assigned to them
findings.evidence: This is the chain's central quantitative defect and it is provable from the database alone before any source is opened. The duration_note attached to link 2, titled 'Strategic ranking (decadal survey or council priority)', reads 'concept studies and three funded teams to selection of the TRW/Ball design'. The duration_note attached to link 3, 'Funding authorisation', reads 'design selection to the start of long-lead construction'. Neither note describes the link it is attached to. I re-derived the intervals independently from STScI's own mission timeline (https://www.stsci.edu/jwst/about-jwst/history/mission-timeline) and from Gardner et al. 2023 (PASP, https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1538-3873/acd1b5/pdf). The 1996-2002 window contains: industry study teams formed 4 June 1997; 'Yardstick Design' report 6 August 1998; NASA selects Lockheed Martin and TRW as contractors 7 July 1999; TRW/Ball design selected and telescope named 10-14 September 2002. There is no decadal-survey or strategic-ranking event in that window at all — JWST's actual decadal endorsement was the McKee-Taylor survey published 2001, which the chain never counts. The 2002-2004 window contains only the run-up to 'Construction begins March 3, 2004'; no appropriation, no new-start authorisation, no funding condition. So 8.0 of the 32.5 years are assigned to two links whose stated blockers ('a fixed external cadence', 'appropriation, and conditions attached to it') did not occur in the intervals assigned, and both of those links carry ai_acts = 0. The evidence fields for both links cite only Rubin and the ELT, never JWST — the chain silently borrows blockers from other programmes and hangs them on JWST segments. This is decisive for the headline: move those 8 years to the design and procurement work the notes actually describe, which is where the chain itself places 'Design and optimization search' with ai_acts = 1, and 'AI acts on 9.5 of the 32.5 years, leaving 23' becomes 'AI acts on 17.5, leaving 15'. The binding-flag circularity was cleared, but the same selection survived one level down, in which label got attached to which interval.

findings.target: path-telescope-elapsed-time, link seq 4 'Design maturation' — interval contradicted by its own evidence field
findings.evidence: Link 4 is assigned 2004-2006, 2.0 years, and carries ai_acts = 1. Its own evidence field ends '...instrument critical design reviews 2006, mission critical design review 2010', so the link's cited evidence runs four years past the interval it is given. Independently confirmed: mission Preliminary Design Review 4 April 2008 (NASA Advisory Council Astrophysics Subcommittee minutes, 10 April 2008, https://science.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/2008_04_FactFindingTelecon_.pdf); project confirmation/KDP-C April 2009 (GAO-13-4 p.4); mission CDR April 2010 (JATIS, 'Lessons learned from systems engineering on JWST'). All three fall inside the window the chain labels 'Fabrication' (link 5, 2006-2011, ai_acts = 0). Design maturation on JWST ran to 2010, not 2006. Taking the link's own cited endpoint gives link 4 six years rather than two, moving a further 4 years into the AI-acts column and the headline residual from 23 to 19 even before finding 1 is applied. Related but lesser: instrument CDRs are not a single year — NIRCam ~May 2006, MIRI optical system CDR May 2007, FGS passed conditionally by early 2008 — so 'instrument critical design reviews 2006' is the earliest of a 2006-2008 spread.

findings.target: path-telescope-elapsed-time, link seq 6 'Integration and test' — blocker 'strictly serial single-string assembly, so nothing can be parallelised'
findings.evidence: My counter-argument for chain 1, and it is the strongest one available. Link 6 is the largest block in the chain (9.0 of 32.5 years, 2011-2020) and carries ai_acts = 0 on the stated ground that the delay is irreducibly physical. The endpoint itself is correct — I initially suspected 2020 was wrong because STScI dates 'final integrated testing completed' to 1 December 2017, but that is the element-level OTIS cryo-vacuum test at Johnson; NASA announced completion of the full observatory's acoustic and sine-vibration environmental testing on 6 October 2020 (https://www.nasa.gov/feature/goddard/2020/nasa-s-james-webb-space-telescope-completes-environmental-testing). So the interval stands. What does not stand is the blocker. GAO-13-4 (3 December 2012, https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-13-4.pdf) p.4, verbatim: 'the JWST project was reauthorized, but not before it was recommended for termination by the House Appropriations Committee... NASA announced that the project would be rebaselined at $8.835 billion — a 78 percent increase — and would launch in October 2018 — a delay of 52 months.' That is 4.3 years of delay arising from a near-termination and a replan, sitting inside the window the chain attributes to serial physical assembly. A second tranche follows: the 2018 Independent Review Board, convened after sunshield tears and loose fasteners that Northrop attributed to workmanship error, moved launch readiness to March 2021 — IRB chair Young described the causes as 'simple fixes' costing roughly 1.5 years and nearly $1B. So the chain's single largest ai_acts = 0 block is substantially funding latency and defect rework, neither of which is 'single-string assembly on hardware that cannot be duplicated'. On the chain's own taxonomy, workmanship-defect detection sits under 'Sensing and signal processing' and a replan under 'Coordination and institutional'. This also breaks the chain's structural model: it places funding authorisation once, early, as a 2-year link, whereas the record shows funding-driven delay recurring mid-build and dominating. A strictly sequential eight-link chain cannot represent that, and the chain does not say so.

findings.target: path-telescope-elapsed-time, links seq 2, 3, 5, 6 — rationale strings still assert the withdrawn binding claim, and the artifact ships them
findings.evidence: is_binding = 0 for all eight chain-1 links, but four rationale strings still open with the withdrawn claim: 'Binding, and binding in an unusual way: the delay is quantised...' (seq 2); 'Binding, and the ELT case is the cleanest instance available anywhere in this analysis...' (seq 3); 'Binding. All three of Convergent's capabilities attached to this gap act here...' (seq 5); 'Binding, and the single longest link in the JWST chain...' (seq 6). app/src/components/Chain.jsx renders {l.rationale} verbatim in the per-link list, and app/src/app/chains/page.jsx states two screens above it: 'I originally called some steps binding and some not. On a strictly sequential chain that is circular... The arithmetic below replaces it.' The shipped artifact therefore withdraws the binding framing and then asserts it four times, while the link table beside it shows no binding tag on any chain-1 row. Note also that the set still named 'Binding' in prose is exactly {2, 3, 5, 6} — precisely the four steps with ai_acts = 0. That is the original circularity, intact in the text, with only the flag column cleared.

findings.target: docs/critical-paths.md and app/src/components/mermaid.js
findings.evidence: `git log --all -- docs/critical-paths.md` returns exactly one commit, 1ed9421 — the doc has never been touched since the original analysis and predates the binding correction entirely. It still states 'Four links bind, and no current AI capability touches any of them', still carries `class L2,L3,L5,L6 binding` in the chain-1 Mermaid, and still puts a filled marker on rows 2, 3, 5 and 6 of the chain-1 link table. It also disagrees with the database on link 7 maturity ('Working now' in the doc, 'Speculative' in the DB) and reports the total as 32 where the DB uses 32.5. app/src/components/mermaid.js carries the identical stale `class L2,L3,L5,L6 binding` line; it is currently imported by nothing, but decisions row 44 records the intent that 'The Mermaid source is in docs/critical-paths.md and in a copy block under each chain', so it is either shipped or about to be. Either file reaching a reader hands them the retracted claim as the current one.

findings.target: path-publishing-cost — the dotted edge 'cheaper drafting adds load' from link 1 to link 3, and the finding 'the labor moved to reviewer recruitment, which is where the cost now concentrates'
findings.evidence: This is chain 2's marquee unpredicted result and its only quantitative support is the Organization Science full-corpus editorial. I read that source. Pierce, Gartenberg, Hasan and Murray, 'More Versus Better: Artificial Intelligence, Incentives, and the Emerging Crisis in Peer Review', Organization Science 2026, doi 10.1287/orsc.2026.ed.v37.n3; editors' summary at https://orgsci.substack.com/p/more-versus-better-part-i. It places the displaced load on editors at desk screening, not on reviewer recruitment: 'Among manuscripts with 70%+ AI scores, nearly 70% are desk-rejected' against 44% for low-AI submissions, and 'editors, all of whom are volunteers with their own research and teaching obligations, are spending a growing share of their time assessing manuscripts.' The essay gives no invitation-rate or recruitment figures at all; on reviewers it says only that the editorial team 'expanded... adding editors and reviewers to absorb the load'. So the arrow the chain draws from link 1 to link 3 is supported by its own source only as an arrow from link 1 to link 2 — a link the chain flags is_binding = 0 and ai_acts = 1 and dismisses as 'genuinely tractable for current models, which is why it is already being done and why it does not set the cost'. On the chain's own stated axis, 'reviewer and editor labour per published paper', a 42% submission surge absorbed by volunteer editors at screening is a cost concentration at link 2, and link 2 is the strongest alternative binding link in chain 2. The arithmetic runs the same way: if acceptance counts hold while submissions rise 42% and the increment is ~70% desk-rejected, editor labour per published paper rises and reviewer labour per published paper barely moves.

findings.target: path-publishing-cost, link seq 3 — blocker 'Willingness to serve, not the ability to identify who should serve. These are different problems and only one of them is a matching problem.'
findings.evidence: The matching/willingness split is the chain's central claim — its own rationale says 'The binding half is the half AI does not touch, which is the whole finding of this chain in one link', and decisions row 41 records that the link boundary was deliberately drawn to carry that split. ESO, the source the chain leans on for it, does not make that split. On the same page that supplies the two quotes the artifact uses (https://www.eso.org/sci/observing/phase1/distributed-peer-review.html), ESO lists as a distinct reason for deploying DPR: 'Because of the large number of proposals, the increasing level of specialisation in the time requests, and the limited number of reviewers who can be managed via the classical panel paradigm, it has become progressively more difficult to find optimal proposal-referee matches.' ESO cites supply and matching side by side; the chain quotes the supply bullet and does not mention the matching bullet, then asserts that matching is not the problem. That is selective quotation on the load-bearing link. There is genuine countervailing evidence the chain could have used — Carpenter and Corvillon, 'Distributed Peer Review at ALMA', arXiv:2606.22160, over 20,000 proposals across 13 cycles, report 'little dependence of perceived review quality on expertise level' — but that is a perceived-quality survey (228 reviewers, 21% response), it is not cited, and it does not license dismissing ESO's own stated matching problem. Either cite ESO on both halves and argue the split, or drop the claim that only one half is a matching problem.

findings.target: The intersection claim — 'Chain 1's links 2 and 3 are an instance of chain 2's links 3 and 4' / 'Telescope time and facility approval are allocated by peer review of proposals' / the A3 → SHARED edge in the intersection Mermaid
findings.evidence: I fetched the primary sources myself. The quotations are accurate and the surrounding facts hold: ESO's DPR page states verbatim 'the load on the panels and the Observing Programmes Committee (OPC) members has become unsustainable', 'it has become progressively harder to find scientists willing to serve in the panels and in the OPC', and 'the introduction of triage (for the bottom 30%) has reduced the panels workload, [but] it has significantly degraded the quality of feedback for the triaged proposals'; each PI reviews ten proposals per proposal submitted; DPR has run since Period 110; Patat et al. 2019, The Messenger 177, 3-13 confirms the Period 103 experiment (eight proposals each, not ten) and the Gemini Fast Turnaround precedent. One attribution fix: the artifact presents these as ESO 'writing' when introducing DPR — they are from ESO's Phase 1 web page, not from the Messenger article or the Kerzendorf/Patat paper, neither of which contains the words 'unsustainable', 'willing' or 'degraded'. What fails is not the quotation but what it is made to carry. The same ESO page states that DPR governs the allocation of telescope observing time, not facility construction decisions. Chain 1's link 2 is a decadal survey or an ESO Council strategic priority and link 3 is appropriation plus a 90%-funding condition — decisions about whether to build and fund a facility. ESO's evidence is about who gets nights on a facility that already exists. The artifact says 'The evidence for this is not an analogy. It is ESO's own stated reason for changing the mechanism' — but bridging observing-time allocation to facility approval is precisely the analogy, and it is the step the evidence does not cover. Link 3 is the unsalvageable half: appropriation is not peer review of proposals under any reading, and the chain's own 'cleanest instance available anywhere in this analysis' for link 3 is the ESO Council's June 2012 condition that contracts above EUR 2 million await 90% funding of EUR 1,083 million at 2012 prices (independently confirmed, green light December 2014) — a financing condition with no panel in it. The Mermaid maps A3 'Funding authorisation' into SHARED 'Peer review of proposals'; that edge should not be drawn. Link 2 is partly defensible — decadal surveys do run expert panels over community white papers, via Science Frontier Panels and Project Prioritization Panels — but membership is by appointment to an ad hoc National Academies committee over a roughly two-year study, not by per-proposal invitation, so the quantities the chain imports from chain 2's link 3 (invitations per accepted review, declining acceptance rates) have no analogue in a decadal panel. Recommendation: keep the intersection, narrow it to link 2 and to observing-time allocation, and say plainly that the facility-funding link is an extrapolation.

findings.target: path-publishing-cost, link seq 4 'Review judgment' — flagged binding on the axis 'Cost, measured as reviewer and editor labour per published paper'
findings.evidence: Every figure attached to link 4 measures judgment reliability, and none is denominated in reviewer or editor labour. I confirmed all of them independently and they are correct: NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment, 203 of 882 duplicated papers with inconsistent outcomes, 23.0% (https://blog.neurips.cc/2021/12/08/the-neurips-2021-consistency-experiment/, arXiv:2306.03262); 25.9% in 2014 on 43 of 166 duplicated papers; roughly half the accepted list changing on a rerun (50.6% in 2021, 49.5% in 2014); and Cortes and Lawrence, arXiv:2109.09774, quoted verbatim and correctly. The pairing of 23% with 26% is the right apples-to-apples comparison and should not be 'corrected' to the widely circulated 57%, which is Eric Price's 2014 blog figure. So the figures are `figure-confirmed`. The problem is that the link's rationale says 'Binding, and unusually well quantified for an institutional link' — what is quantified is disagreement, not cost. A link cannot bind a cost axis on accuracy evidence. Either supply a labour figure for link 4, or restate it as binding on a reliability axis that the chain has explicitly excluded. One nuance to carry if the Cortes and Lawrence line is kept: the abstract says 'a correlation' for rejected papers, but the body twice calls it weak.

findings.target: path-publishing-cost, link seq 2 evidence — "ESO reports that classical triage 'has significantly degraded the quality of feedback for the triaged proposals' — screening under load trades feedback quality for throughput."
findings.evidence: The quote is verbatim and correctly attributed to ESO. It crosses two boundaries at once. First it is a quality claim deployed on a cost axis: the rationale it supports reads 'Not binding on the cost axis. Screening is genuinely tractable for current models, which is why it is already being done and why it does not set the cost' — the quote says nothing about tractability or cost, it says triage degrades feedback. Second it is observatory telescope-time proposal triage imported to support a claim about journal desk screening, in the same chain that excludes speed on the explicit ground that 'journal latency is reviewer-supply-driven while conference latency is set by a fixed programme committee calendar, so a chain mixing them would produce a cost concentration that is an artifact of the venue mix'. A chain that refuses to mix journal and conference venues should not silently mix journals with an observatory.

findings.target: path-publishing-cost — the axis choice itself, 'Cost, measured as reviewer and editor labour per published paper'
findings.evidence: Convergent's gap text reads: 'Expensive publishing practices restrict and slow the spread of knowledge. We should replace outdated publishing practices and complement research practices with new approaches that leverage frugal innovation, community-led platforms, and open access. We imagine a future where scientific discovery is more inclusive and dynamic.' The 'expensive' in their sentence is article processing charges and access cost; 'inclusive' is named twice. The chain defines cost as unpaid reviewer and editor labour and excludes inclusiveness — moving the axis off the component the gap statement is about and onto the one component that is not actually expensed, which is also the component where the binding links come out institutional. The producer sees this and says so honestly in link 6's rationale ('this deserves care because it is the link their gap sentence centres on. On the inclusiveness axis — explicitly excluded from this chain — it may well be binding'), and the methodology does require picking one axis and naming the others, which was done. But the binding set is downstream of the axis choice, and the axis chosen is not the gap's own centre of gravity. That should be stated where the finding is stated, not only in a link rationale behind a disclosure toggle. Counter-argument the producer should answer: define cost per published paper in dollars actually paid — the natural reading of 'expensive' — and link 6 binds while links 3, 4 and 7 do not, because unpriced labour has zero accounting cost.

findings.target: path-publishing-cost, link seq 7 'Credit and legitimacy' — flagged binding
findings.evidence: Its own figure field concedes 'no published quantity, the blocker is what committees agree to count', so it binds a cost axis with no cost quantity. Its mechanism, stated in the rationale, is that 'the labour is unpriced and uncredited, and pricing it is an institutional act' — that is, link 7 acts on cost only by way of link 3's reviewer supply. But the chain is drawn as a strictly sequential 1 through 7 with link 7 last, so the DAG does not represent the causality the rationale asserts, and on that causality link 7 is not independently binding: it is link 3's constraint counted a second time. A related inconsistency: link 5 'Editorial decision' is demoted with 'Its cost is largely inherited from link 3', but inheritance is not applied to links 4 or 7, whose costs are inherited from link 3 by the same argument. Applied consistently, the inheritance rule collapses chain 2's binding set to link 3 alone; applied as written, it is used once, to demote one link.

findings.target: path-publishing-cost — pre-registration quality, as distinct from pre-registration ordering
findings.evidence: The ordering is genuine (see prereg block) and I am not contesting it. Two things a sceptical reader will notice and the artifact should pre-empt. First, chain 2's expectation already contains a finding-shaped citation — 'there is published evidence that traditional statistical representations outperform generative AI at identifying expert reviewers' — so the producer held the chain's key piece of evidence at pre-registration time. It is disclosed rather than hidden, which is to the producer's credit, but 'recorded before the link analysis' means less when the evidence was already in hand. Second, and more substantive, the expectation names the three links that would later be flagged binding — 'reviewer recruitment, judgment consistency and the credit and legitimacy step remain untouched' — and the decomposition written afterwards contains exactly seven links of which exactly those three (seq 3, 4, 7) are flagged. Git proves the prediction preceded the decomposition, but the producer chose the number of links and where their boundaries fell while holding the prediction, and decisions row 41 records exactly that for link 3: the boundary was drawn to carry the split 'because the whole finding of the chain lives in the split'. A 3-of-3 hit where the predictor controls the partition is weak confirmation. Recommend saying so in the artifact rather than letting a reader find it. Separately: the gap between the two commits is four minutes thirty-seven seconds, which is fine for an agent but means the two writes came from one continuous context — the git order is evidence about the writes, not about the reasoning, and the artifact currently presents it as though it settles the question.

findings.target: Phase 5 evidence trail — search_log and research-log/searches/
findings.evidence: `select count(*) from search_log` returns 0 for every phase, and there is no research-log/searches/phase-5.json (only phase-3.json exists). Mode C step 2 asks the reviewer to argue an alternative binding link 'using the same evidence base the producer used', and that evidence base is not recoverable — I had to rebuild it from scratch, which is why this review took longer than it should and why I cannot certify that no contrary source was seen and dropped. CLAUDE.md is explicit that the cache is 'what lets the auditor see exactly the evidence the labeler saw, and what makes an honest null provable rather than asserted'. Compounding this, decisions row 39 records that chain 2 was ultimately 'built from its named source of record' on Notion, with the note that the public sources are 'citable in the artifact and the page is not'. So chain 2's evidence base is partly a document neither a reviewer nor a reader at Convergent can open. The chain-1 evidence appears to trace to the phase-3 Brave results (NASA mission timeline, Webb project history, and two Wikipedia JWST timelines) rather than to STScI, GAO or NASA OIG, which is consistent with the label errors in findings 1 and 2 — duration_basis claims the figures come from 'the published milestone record', and the milestone record was not actually read.

findings.target: 'submissions rose 42% over five years in the one corpus where a journal has published full figures' (critical_paths.finding, link 1 evidence and rationale, docs/critical-paths.md, app/src/app/page.jsx)
findings.evidence: The source says: 'Submission volume at Organization Science has risen by 42% since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, compared to the prior two-year window.' The five years is the span of the corpus (6,957 submissions from 11,887 authors, 10,389 reviews by 2,519 reviewers), not the growth period. The growth period is roughly three and a quarter years measured against a two-year baseline. The correction runs in the producer's favour and should be made for that reason: tying the rise to ChatGPT's release is a far stronger warrant for the causal claim than a bare five-year trend, and the source supports it — submissions below 15% AI detection have declined since late 2022, so the increment is essentially all AI-assisted. Suggested restatement: 'submissions rose 42% after ChatGPT's release relative to the prior two-year window, within a five-year full-submission corpus'. Note that the same source's desk-rejection finding cuts against how the 42% is used — see the blocking finding on the link 1 to link 3 edge.

findings.target: 'Roughly five invitations per accepted review (Silverchair, Future of Peer Review 2026)'
findings.evidence: Silverchair's own figure is 4.5, not five: 'It now takes editors an average of 4.5 invitations to secure a single review, nearly double the rate from 2018' (https://www.silverchair.com/news/the-numbers-behind-the-noise/; report at https://www.silverchair.com/news/future-of-peer-review-2026/, based on eight years of ScholarOne Manuscripts activity plus 2,000+ survey responses). Rounding 4.5 up to 'roughly five' on a supply-strain statistic invites exactly the reader who checks. Two stronger unused figures from the same source: reviewer acceptance fell from 43% in 2018 to 22% in 2024, and 'per 100 invitations sent, editors wait a combined 407 days for reviewers who ultimately say no or say nothing at all' — the second is denominated in time, which is what the cost axis needs.

findings.target: 'A survey of 139 journal editors with 27 interviews finds 55% rate finding reviewers a significant or very significant challenge' (Jamali, Luca and Wakeling)
findings.evidence: Every number is right and the quote about 30 or more invitations to secure two reviewers is verbatim, dated 15 February 2026. Two scope corrections. The respondents are editors of Australian journals, largely local and society titles — 'a survey of 139 journal editors' generalises a national sample of small journals to journal editing at large, and small local journals are precisely where reviewer recruitment is hardest, so the direction of the bias favours the chain's conclusion. And the cited item is The Conversation, a popular-press piece (https://theconversation.com/the-peer-review-system-is-breaking-down-heres-how-we-can-fix-it-275317); the peer-reviewed underpinnings are Jamali et al., Learned Publishing 2026, doi 10.1002/leap.2034 and Luca et al., doi 10.1002/leap.2041, which is what should be cited.

findings.target: 'Meyerson documents 21 years of declining reviewer acceptance, 2002-2024'
findings.evidence: Meyerson, Suzzi-Simmons and Simberloff (2025), 'Quantifying reviewer declines in scientific publishing: twenty-one years of data from biological invasions 2002-2024', Biological Invasions 27(10), doi 10.1007/s10530-025-03679-1. The finding is real. Two caveats the chain does not carry: it is editorial data from a single journal, Biological Invasions, and the sentence as written reads as a field-wide result; and the paper is internally inconsistent about its own window, the title saying 2002-2024 and the abstract saying 2003 to 2024. The chain follows the title, which is defensible, but a reader who opens it will find the discrepancy.

findings.target: 'traditional statistical representations outperform generative AI at identifying expert peer reviewers, tested on NASA/ADS records and observatory DPR data across 379 researchers'
findings.evidence: Fully verified, including the figure I most expected to be loose. Amado Olivo, Jerabkova, Klencki, Carpenter, Malicki, Patat, Strolger and Kerzendorf, arXiv:2605.18752, 18 May 2026. TF-IDF placed a labelled expert in the top 25 recommendations 79.5% of the time against 51.5% for GPT-4o mini across six retrieval methods. The 379 is exact — 'the 435 submissions resulted in a final pool of 379 unique reviewers' — the data is the ESO Period 110 DPR call with 4,350 reviewer-proposal assignments and self-reported expertise as ground truth, and reviewer publication profiles were retrieved through the NASA/ADS API. One caveat worth carrying, because the chain leans on this to set link 3's maturity and to claim AI 'reaches the tractable half': the generative baseline tested is GPT-4o mini, a budget model, so the result is a statement about one cheap model in a retrieval task, not a ceiling on generative methods. Also, over 90% of the 379 are proposal PIs rather than an independent reviewer pool.

findings.target: path-telescope-elapsed-time, programmes_json and duration_basis — the ELT and Rubin figures and the '32.5 against STScI's stated 32'
findings.evidence: Checked and correct. The ELT claim, which the chain calls its cleanest instance, holds almost verbatim: the ESO Council approved construction in June 2012 on the condition that contracts above EUR 2 million could be awarded only once the total cost of EUR 1,083 million at 2012 prices was 90% funded, and the green light followed in December 2014 after Poland's accession. STScI does publish the total: 'From conception to launch of the James Webb Space Telescope took 32 years', and the September 1989 workshop is confirmed as 13-15 September 1989 at STScI. Three small corrections. Site civil works began with a groundbreaking ceremony in June 2014 under an explicit exception to the contract condition, so 'roughly two and a half years of pure funding latency with the design frozen' is closer to two years of frozen procurement. STScI's 32 runs conception to launch while the chain's eight links run to first light in July 2022, so the 32.5 sum and the 32 measure different endpoints — the agreement is presented as corroboration but is not one, and docs/critical-paths.md and the database disagree with each other (32 vs 32.5) on the same quantity. And the decadal survey the chain never counts is conventionally 'the 2000 decadal survey', published 2001; if it is added, say which.

findings.target: 'Your export has one row per gap and nowhere to record that.' (app/src/app/chains/page.jsx)
findings.evidence: Second person, and it tells the reader their artifact lacks something. methodology/critical-path.md requires the observation frame: "'None of the three listed capabilities acts on the approval link' is an observation. 'They missed the real bottleneck' is a critique, and it loses the reader in one sentence." The same content survives the reframe intact — a chain has somewhere to record that two gaps share a blocker; a row per gap does not — which is the test that this is a wording problem rather than a substance problem. docs/critical-paths.md carries the same sentence as 'A catalogue cannot show this: it has one row per gap and no place to record that two rows are blocked by the same thing.'

findings.target: 'That is a natural experiment in review capacity under load, at scale, with a before and after, and as far as I can find nobody funds it as research.' (app/src/app/chains/page.jsx; same sentence in docs/critical-paths.md)
findings.evidence: Addressed to an organisation whose business is deciding what research to fund, 'nobody funds it as research' reads as 'you are not funding the obvious thing', and it is the last sentence before the contact line, so it is where the reader is left. It is also the one claim in the intersection section with no source behind it — an absence of funding established by not having found any. Recommend either dropping the clause or stating it as an offer: this is a natural experiment with a before and after, and it is the kind of thing chains are good at surfacing.

findings.target: 'those three are aimed at 14 of the 23 years AI does not reach, which is a better hit rate than three picked at random would manage.' (critical_paths.finding, chain 1)
findings.evidence: Benchmarking their capability selection against chance is faint praise, and a reader at Convergent will hear it as such. The preceding sentence — 'The prediction about your capability set holds exactly' — already makes the point, and the sentence before that names the three capabilities and where they act, which is the observation the methodology asks for. The random-baseline comparison adds no information and costs goodwill.

findings.target: app/src/app/chains/page.jsx — section heading 'Both chains share a binding step'
findings.evidence: The same page states two paragraphs earlier that the binding framing was withdrawn for the sequential chain because it is circular, then heads the intersection section with 'binding step' and, in the finding text, calls chain 1's ranking and funding links binding by implication. Chain 1 now has zero links flagged binding in the database, so 'both chains share a binding step' is not true of the data as it stands. This also costs the pair its stated design: methodology/critical-path.md specifies 'one where the binding links turn out to be physical, one where they turn out to be institutional', and after the correction all three binding flags in the project sit in chain 2, so the physical half of the contrast has no binding link to point at. The arithmetic reframing is the right fix for the circularity, but the pair's discrimination claim needs restating in the new vocabulary rather than left half-converted.

summary: Pre-registration is real and I could not break it: bbfa54f (14:04:32) carries both expectations with finding null and links empty, and 1ed9421 (14:09:09) adds the analysis, with chain 1's expectation text byte-identical to the database. Everything else went worse. The binding-flag circularity was cleared in the flag column but survives in three places the correction did not reach: four chain-1 rationale strings still open with the word 'Binding' and the artifact renders them verbatim beneath the paragraph withdrawing the claim, docs/critical-paths.md has never been touched since the original commit and still asserts 'Four links bind', and the set still named binding in prose is exactly the four steps with ai_acts = 0 — the original circularity, intact, with only the flag cleared. Worse, the same selection reappears one level down in the arithmetic that replaced it: chain 1's link 2 is titled 'Strategic ranking' over an interval its own note describes as contractor competition, link 3 is titled 'Funding authorisation' over an interval its own note describes as design work, and STScI's milestone record confirms there is no ranking or appropriation event in either window — so 8 of the 32.5 years reach the ai_acts = 0 column by labelling, and link 4's own evidence field runs to a 2010 mission CDR four years past the interval it is given; correcting either moves the headline from 'leaving 23' toward 15. Chain 2 fares no better on its two load-bearing claims: the dotted 'cheaper drafting adds load' edge to reviewer recruitment is contradicted by the Organization Science editorial it cites, which puts the displaced load on volunteer editors at desk screening (nearly 70% of high-AI submissions desk-rejected) — a link the chain calls non-binding and AI-tractable — and the matching-versus-willingness split is contradicted by ESO's own DPR page, which names difficulty finding optimal proposal-referee matches as a separate reason for DPR in the bullet list immediately beside the two bullets the artifact quotes. The intersection quotations are all verbatim and correct, but ESO's page states DPR governs allocation of telescope observing time, not facility construction decisions, so the edge from chain 1's funding link into 'peer review of proposals' should not be drawn; narrow the intersection to the ranking link and to time allocation, and it survives. Six blocking findings, and I would not ship the chains page until the first five are cleared; the tone flags ('Your export has one row per gap and nowhere to record that', 'nobody funds it as research', 'better than three picked at random') are all one-sentence rewrites that keep the content. One note on the review brief itself: it pointed me at Kevin Heng for the DPR literature and no such work exists — DPR originates with Merrifield and Saari (2009), which Patat et al. cite, and the repo never claimed otherwise, so this is not a finding against the producer.
